title: How to Get Unstuck From Analysis Paralysis
summary: Research that started as care can turn into a way to avoid choosing. Sort one-way from two-way doors, ask what would change your mind, and run a timeboxed spike.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Day three of picking a charting library for the new dashboard. You have fourteen tabs open: three blog posts comparing the same two libraries, a GitHub issue thread from 2022, two pricing pages and a spreadsheet with 22 rows of criteria. You haven't written a line of code. You haven't ruled anything out either. It all feels so responsible.

That's what makes analysis paralysis sneaky. It looks like diligence from the outside, and for a while it is. This post is about how to notice when research has stopped helping, how to tell big decisions from small ones, and how to get unstuck with something small and real.

When research stops helping

The instinct behind it is good. You want to understand the options, avoid mistakes you could have avoided and respect what a decision costs. In engineering that instinct saves you from migrations that hurt users and abstractions that trap the team for years.

The shift is hard to see. At first you gather information to make the decision. Later you gather it to put off the discomfort of making it. The calendar still says "research," the notes keep growing and the wording still sounds thoughtful. The difference is that every new tab makes the choice feel heavier and no clearer.

One question cuts through it: could the next piece of information actually change what I pick? If yes, go get it. If you'd pick the same library no matter what the next blog post says, more reading only adds texture. Most decisions never reach certainty. They reach "good enough to try, watch and adjust."

One-way doors and two-way doors

Jeff Bezos gave this idea its best-known shape in his 2015 letter to Amazon shareholders. Some decisions are one-way doors: consequential and hard or impossible to reverse, so they deserve to be made "methodically, carefully, slowly." Most decisions are two-way doors. If you pick badly, you can walk back through. His warning was about what happens as organizations grow: they start using the slow, heavy process for the reversible decisions too, and the result is "slowness, unthoughtful risk aversion, failure to experiment sufficiently."

The 2016 letter added a rule of thumb: most decisions should probably be made with somewhere around 70% of the information you wish you had, and if you wait for 90%, you're probably being slow. The reasoning that goes with it matters more than the number: if you're good at course correcting, being wrong may cost less than you think, while being slow is expensive for sure.

Back to the dashboard. Changing the data model or signing a three-year vendor contract is a one-way door. A charting library used in one screen, behind a small wrapper, is a two-way door. Treating it like a one-way door is how day one turns into day three. There's a whole post on this in Find the Way Back Before You Decide.

Swap reading for a spike

Extreme Programming has a name for the way out: a spike solution, a very simple program built only to explore one tough technical question. It ignores every other concern, and you should expect to throw it away. Its job is to reduce risk.

For the dashboard, that means giving each library a two-hour timebox to render your real data in your real layout. Two hours of contact with reality will usually settle what three days of comparison tables couldn't. Other versions of the same move: run the query on production-sized data, interview two users, or write the proposal and ask one reviewer to tear it apart.

Keep the decision note short

A decision note helps, as long as it stays on one screen:

  • What are we deciding, in one sentence?
  • Which options are still alive?
  • What matters most here: cost, speed, safety, maintainability or how easy it is to reverse?
  • What would make us change our mind?
  • What's the smallest next step, and when do we check the result?

If the note keeps growing, it has become tab number fifteen. A good one cuts noise.

The fear underneath

Sometimes the option isn't what scares you. What scares you is being the person who picked it if it goes wrong. That's why the team around you matters so much. If every imperfect decision ends in blame, people learn to hide behind more analysis. If decisions are treated as owned experiments that get reviewed honestly, people move earlier.

Being decisive is different from being rushed. Rushing ignores evidence. Deciding well looks at the evidence, names what's still unknown and picks a next step anyway: here's what we know, here's what we don't, here's why this option makes sense today and here's how we'll notice if it's wrong. If you want more on living with the part that's still unknown, try this post on carrying uncertainty.

Try this week

  • Take the decision you've been circling and write it in one sentence.
  • Label it a one-way door or a two-way door. If it's two-way, give it a deadline measured in days.
  • Write down the one fact that would change your mind. If no fact would, stop researching.
  • Close half your tabs and timebox a spike instead.

faqs.a: It's when gathering information stops helping you decide and becomes a way to put the decision off. A good check: if the next piece of information couldn't change your choice, you're probably stuck rather than researching.

faqs.q: What are one-way and two-way door decisions?
faqs.a: Jeff Bezos described them in his 2015 shareholder letter. One-way doors are hard or impossible to reverse and deserve a slow, careful process. Two-way doors can be undone if you choose badly, so they should be made quickly by individuals or small groups.

faqs.q: How much information do you need before deciding?
faqs.a: Bezos's rule of thumb from his 2016 letter is about 70% of the information you wish you had. Waiting for 90% usually means you're being slow, especially when you're good at noticing and correcting a wrong call.

faqs.q: What is a spike in software development?
faqs.a: A term from Extreme Programming: a very simple, throwaway program written to answer one tough technical question and reduce risk. Timebox it, run it against real data where you can, and use the result to make the decision.
